analysis.one_liner: Bans treating fine print on a cashed check as your authorization for automatic withdrawals.
analysis.headline: The consumer protection bill never left a House subcommittee and died when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993, without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: At the time, companies could hand consumers checks — rebate checks, loan proceeds, prize checks — with fine print stating that cashing or depositing the check counted as agreeing to recurring electronic withdrawals from their bank account. This bill would amend the Electronic Fund Transfer Act to say that endorsing, depositing, or otherwise negotiating a check can never count as authorization for a preauthorized or other electronic transfer, and that no language printed on a check can create that authorization. It was introduced by Rep. Bruce Vento with 32 cosponsors and referred to the House Banking Committee on March 19, 1991; four years of the Congress passed with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers who cash rebate, loan, or prize checks without realizing the fine print enrolls them in recurring debits. Under the bill, a bank could not pull money from their account on the basis of a check endorsement, and no printed provision on a check could serve as their authorization [S3]. The Federal Reserve would write regulations to enforce the rule [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Consumers cashing checks with hidden terms

how_it_helps.text: Adds a subsection to the Electronic Fund Transfer Act barring any preauthorized or other electronic fund transfer made on the basis of a consumer's endorsement, deposit, or negotiation of a check [S3].
Provides that no provision printed on a check may be treated as the consumer's authorization for electronic transfers, closing the fine-print loophole [S3].
Applies immediately upon enactment to any electronic transfer made after that date, regardless of when the underlying check was negotiated [S3].
Directs the Federal Reserve Board to prescribe regulations needed to carry out the prohibition [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Banks and lenders that used check-endorsement fine print to claim customers had agreed to recurring electronic withdrawals would lose that method of obtaining authorization, and companies selling memberships or services on that basis would lose their collection channel [S3].
analysis.who_pays_short: Banks and subscription sellers using check fine print

drawbacks.text: The bill as drafted bars any electronic transfer based on check negotiation, which could also sweep in situations where a consumer knowingly and deliberately authorizes a recurring payment by endorsing a document, leaving businesses without a check-based authorization method and pushing disputes to regulator-written rules [S3].
The prohibition applies retroactively in effect — to transfers made after enactment regardless of when the check was endorsed — which could generate litigation over pre-existing arrangements [S3].

Because the underlying problem is disclosure and consent, an honest objection is that the bill eliminates a mechanism some consumers did use intentionally, rather than requiring clearer affirmative consent [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to ordinary consumers is direct and concrete: money could no longer be pulled from their accounts on the strength of fine print they never read. The costs fall on specific firms that relied on that mechanism, and the main design weakness — no clear alternative path for genuine check-based authorizations — was left to Federal Reserve rulemaking. On balance the bill's purpose was protective, but it died without refinement or debate.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in March 1991, referred to the House Banking Committee and then to its Consumer Affairs and Coinage Subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended in January 1993 without any hearing, markup, or vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Bruce Vento introduced the Account Fraud and Deception Prevention Act of 1991 on March 19, 1991, with 32 original cosponsors [S5].
The bill was referred the same day to the House Committee on Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs [S5].
On April 1, 1991, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage, the last action ever taken on it [S5].
No further action occurred before the 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill never received a vote in committee or on the House floor [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Banks and sellers that used fine print on checks to claim authorization for recurring electronic withdrawals kept the practice, and consumers continued to bear the risk of unauthorized debits.

for.name: Rep. Bruce Vento
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 19, 1991 to close the check fine-print loophole in the Electronic Fund Transfer Act.

for.name: 32 of 435 House representatives
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, including the chair of the Consumer Affairs subcommittee to which it was referred.

against.name: House Subcommittee on Consumer Affairs and Coinage
against.role: Subcommittee of the House Banking, Finance and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on April 1, 1991 and never scheduled a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All 32 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's Independent (Bernie Sanders); no Republicans signed on, and the bill died in a Democratic-led subcommittee without opposition ever being recorded.

industries.note: The bill would have barred them from treating a customer's cashing of a check — often a rebate or loan check carrying fine print — as consent to recurring electronic withdrawals, removing a tool for converting one-time transactions into ongoing debits from consumers' accounts.
Sellers that distributed teaser checks whose fine print enrolled consumers in paid memberships funded by automatic debits would lose that enrollment and billing channel entirely.
